MorphoHand · real_v1 · 16 September 2026

Basketball grasp on the real_v1 hand: reach, seating and held lift across three gantry layouts

A size-7 basketball is reachable on the real_v1 hand only as a friction cap grasp from above, at wrap angles up to 65° on the widest gantry layout, with the ball 18 mm short of the palm plate. With the measured servo (0.35 N m, 3–8 N per pad) it holds a 0.10 m lift only from μ 1.0 at θ 65°; the shipped kp 30 servo holds it from μ 0.6. Seating the ball against the plate needs a mount ring 5 mm wider than the gantries reach. A size-3 ball on the same layout wraps to θ 90°, seats against the plate and holds from μ 0.6, the lowest tested.

880 close–lift–hold rollouts over 44 fitted grasps · 3 gantry layouts · ball sizes 3, 5, 6, 7 · shipped and measured servo · scripts/real_v1_basketball_grasp.py

The palm plate moved 25 mm up, and what that buys

assets/mjcf/real_v1 · PALM_PLATE_Z in build_real_v1_scenes.py

The flat palm of the physical hand sits 25 mm above the plane the three yaw servos are mounted on; until today the simulated plate was drawn on the mounting plane itself, 25 mm too close to the fingertips. The plate geom and the workspace sites now sit at +25 mm in the palm frame. Nothing else moved: mounts, link lengths, ROM and the 21 contact excludes are the CAD numbers, and the fitted open_ik keys of the screwdriver scene were carried through the rebuild (--keep-keyframes). Scenes generated before 2026-09-16 still carry the old plate.

For a ball the plate matters because a ball pressed against it cannot sag. A ball seated on the plate's underside puts its centre 96.5 mm below the mounting plane for size 7, and its cross-section at the foot of the yaw links is then wider than the ring the three mounts sit on: the links need a ring of at least 107.8 mm for size 7, 105.7 mm for size 6, 102.4 mm for size 5 and 90.0 mm for size 3. The widest legal layout, every gantry at the end of its travel, rings the ball at 102.6 mm. The nominal layout rings it at 65.1 mm and the bench's best-retaining deployed hand, g12, at 51.9 mm.

What the fingers can reach on the ball

forward-kinematic reach map on a 69 × 55 × 38 joint grid per finger, links clear of the ball

A pad on the upper cap at polar angle θ from the top pole pushes the ball down by N cosθ and its friction lifts by at most μN sinθ, so a pad carries weight only once tanθ > 1/μ: 45° at μ 1.0, 59° at μ 0.6. The finger reaches outboard of its own mount by at most the 15° of MCP extension, and the contact ring at θ sits outboard of the mounts once (R + 10.55 mm) sinθ exceeds the mount ring, which on the wide layout is θ = 52° for size 7. Past that the palm has to climb until the fingers are near full extension, and the plate gap grows. The table gives, per layout and size, the largest wrap angle at which all three pads land with the thumb on its meridian and the pair mirrored near ±60°, and the palm height that puts the ball nearest the plate at that angle.

Held lift under the shipped and the measured servo

close 2 s · lift 0.10 m over 1.5 s (smoothstep) · hold 2 s · held = ball within 20 mm of the lift, slip < 20 mm

80 of the 220 measured-servo rollouts at a saturating command hold the lift. On the wide layout and a size-7 ball the hold starts at μ 1.0 and θ 65°, with 5.7 N per pad at the end of the hold and the friction cone 90% used. Below that friction the ball stays on the floor: the pads’ normal forces push it down by N cosθ and the friction cannot lift more than μN sinθ. A 10 mm position command on the measured servo is only 0.15 N m, under the cliff, and holds nothing.

green = held, with the mean pad normal force at the end of the hold; red = dropped; grey = no reachable grasp at that wrap angle.

The shipped servo is a control: kp 30 with a 10 N m ceiling presses 50–150 N per pad, which no finger on the bench delivers, and its column says only that the geometry admits a hold when force is free. The measured column is the one a plan on the CB1 would see. Smaller balls wrap further and hold at lower friction; size 3 is the first whose equator the pads reach, and at the equator the ball seats against the plate. Nothing past the equator is reachable on any layout.

The friction constraint decides the outcome at the repo's default contact settings

cone and impratio in <option>

The wide / size 7 / θ 65° grasp is repeated below under both settings. 4 of 4 cases drop at the default and hold at the grasp setting, and the closing force is the same either way: at settle the index pad carries 32–35 N under the shipped servo and 6 N under the measured one. What differs is whether that force survives the first millimetre of lift.

Every real_v1 scene in this repo runs the default. The pinch grasps it was tuned on do not care, because their normals oppose each other and friction carries only the weight. A cap grasp carries the normals’ downward component on friction as well, so the frictional impedance sets whether the pads keep their 0.5–1 mm of penetration through the first millimetre of lift. The rows above are the grasp setting; the default is reported here as the sensitivity, and the bench decides which one the pads follow.

What this does not settle

  • The pad–ball friction coefficient. The hold on a size-7 ball needs μ ≥ 1.0 at the measured servo torque; rubber on the TPU pad is probably 0.8–1.5 and has never been measured. Drag a pad across an inflated ball under a known normal load with the bench scale; one number moves this from feasible to infeasible.
  • The servo’s force at the pad. The measured plant delivers 3–8 N per pad here, from kp 0.5 and the 0.35 N m cliff fitted on the screwdriver deficits. Press a pad on the scale at a saturating command (any joint error over 0.7 rad) and read it directly.
  • The approach. Every rollout starts with the pads 8 mm off the ball at the fitted pose. Descending onto the ball from above lands the thumb on the cap before the pair are round it; that sequence needs the arm and is not simulated.
  • Pad and ball compliance. Rigid pads on a rigid sphere with MuJoCo’s soft constraints. A TPU pad flattening on an inflated ball adds contact area and torsional resistance the model does not have; both help a cap grasp.
  • Seating a size-7 ball. Needs a mount ring of 107.8 mm against the 102.6 mm the gantries reach, 5 mm short on each finger. Size 5 clears the links by 0.2 mm on paper and no fitted grasp seated it; size 3 seats at θ 90°. The next measurement is the gantry travel itself: 6 mm more on each axis would seat a size-7 ball, and the CAD workspace boxes are the only record of the limit.
